v: **Verdict.** At commit `125e9e5` GnB-SMH is not safe to secure value on a public network. The audit confirmed **5 Critical** and **19 High** findings, all five re-verified in the code by the lead auditor and each demonstrated by an executable proof-of-concept test. On a weighted, code-only scorecard GnB-SMH scores **3.1 / 10** against **9.1 / 10** for Bitcoin Core.

The cryptographic and arithmetic building blocks are good and, in places, exemplary; the failures are in how blocks and transactions flow through the node: what state a block is validated against, what a peer can make a node do before any proof of work is checked, and what the miner assembles.

**Proof-of-work arithmetic is exact.** The compact-target codec accepts and decodes exactly what Bitcoin Core accepts across all 587,202,560 values with a decodable exponent; ASERT is bit-identical to the aserti3-2d fixed-point construction on more than 350,000 cases; GnB-SMH in Rust equals the normative Python definition on 103 inputs; timestamps are bounded so that timewarp is impossible (better than Bitcoin mainnet today).

**Signatures are combined correctly.** The hybrid scheme requires both ML-DSA-65 and Falcon-1024, parses every component at exact length, uses the constant-time integer Falcon variant, fails closed on randomness errors, and binds the sighash to a domain and a chain id.

**Arithmetic hygiene and memory safety.** Value sums use checked arithmetic throughout (CVE-2010-5139, CVE-2012-2459 and CVE-2018-17144 classes are covered); consensus crates forbid `unsafe`; production code has 3 `unsafe` sites, all FFI; release builds keep overflow checks.

**The existing tests pass.** 1,040 test executions in 61 binaries, the standalone crate, the vendored guards (in isolation) and the Python references all pass. The ledger-v1 sparse Merkle tree prototype showed no soundness defect.

**Consensus state model (DAG-1, VAL-2, VAL-3, DAG-6).** Every block, including parallel DAG blocks, is validated against the node's current tip UTXO set, so two honest nodes that see two sibling blocks containing the same mempool transaction in opposite order reject each other's branch forever. Duplicate coinbases, same-block coinbase spends and a node-local reorg cap add miner-triggerable splits.

**Unauthenticated network denial of service (POW-2, NET-2).** One gossip frame with `height = u64::MAX` panics the block processor on every node it reaches; junk blocks are relayed before validation and each costs every node a full 64 MiB proof-of-work evaluation (~0.8 s) against attacker-chosen bits, with no penalty.

**Block production liveness (MEM-1, MEM-2).** A single gossiped dust transaction, or about 116 ordinary pending transactions, makes every template produced by the stock miner and `getblocktemplate` consensus-invalid.

**Assurance.** CI never compiles or tests the node workspace, there is no fuzzing harness, one test file is compiled out, feature unification disables the real ASERT path in workspace tests, and the dependency policy fails its own checks.

v: The audit covers the complete repository at commit `125e9e5` and compares it with Bitcoin Core master at commit `f13ae51`. It is **code-only**: findings and scores are based on source code, tests and tool output. Nothing in this report depends on hashrate, miner or user adoption, market conditions, decentralisation, or other properties that only exist once a network is used; where an attack needs proof of work, the report states the work required by the code (for example, one evaluation at the pow limit) rather than its cost in hardware.

**Manual review.** Seven reviewers each read every line of one area: proof of work and difficulty; GhostDAG, chain selection and reorganisation; block and transaction validation, UTXO set and storage; cryptography and signatures; P2P, sync, RPC and explorer; wallets and web front end; mempool, shielded pool, attestation, ledger v1 and deployment. Each finding is traced to `file:line` and labelled *Confirmed by test*, *Confirmed by reading* or *Plausible*.

**Verification.** Every Critical finding and the High findings that drive the verdict were re-read in the code by the lead auditor; duplicates reported by several reviewers were merged and are marked as independently reproduced. Severities were calibrated across areas.

**Execution.** All of GnB's own suites were built and run in release mode, plus 73 proof-of-concept tests written during the audit (Appendix C explains how to run them; they live in `audit/poc` so that they do not alter the project's suites).

**Independent consistency testing.** A separate crate, `audit/consistency`, applies Bitcoin Core's own vectors, line-for-line ports of Core and BCHN routines, and rust-bitcoin as oracles to GnB's consensus arithmetic (Section 5).
**Mutation testing and dependency audit.** cargo-mutants on the PoW and difficulty crate; cargo-audit against the RustSec database of 14 October 2026; cargo-deny against the project's own policy.
**Bitcoin Core comparison.** For each component the corresponding Core files, tests, fuzz targets and CI jobs at `f13ae51` were identified and counted directly from the source tree.

v: The scorecard (Section 9) has nine categories weighted by their importance to the safety of a proof-of-work currency node. Each reviewer scored its component 0-10 for GnB and for the matching Bitcoin Core component; the lead auditor calibrated these against the findings and positive controls. Bitcoin Core was not re-audited: its scores reflect the code, tests and CI present at `f13ae51` and its known open issues (for example, the timewarp mitigation is not active on mainnet).
No live network was attacked. Network findings were demonstrated in-process or with local multi-node swarms.

`accept_block` and the message processor live in the node binary (`main.rs`) and cannot be linked from tests. Two proof-of-concept files therefore contain a verbatim copy of that code, guarded by a test that checks the copy line by line against `main.rs`.
No formal verification and no review of third-party crates beyond the advisory database and the FFI boundary of the post-quantum libraries.
Timings were measured on a shared 4-core container and are indicative only.

GnB is a hard fork of the Bloch BlockDAG node. It keeps Bloch's block format, GhostDAG consensus (k = 10), UTXO transaction model, hybrid ML-DSA-65 + Falcon-1024 signatures and libp2p network stack, replaces the proof of work with GnB-SMH (a sequential memory-hard SHAKE-256 function using 64 MiB per evaluation) and ASERT difficulty, and starts from a genesis that carries over the Bloch Genesis-3 ledger. A shielded pool, remote attestation and a stateless ledger (v1) are present but inactive in consensus.

GnB is roughly a seventh of Bitcoin Core's size, but the BlockDAG adds machinery (coloring, reachability, mergesets, multi-parent templates) that a longest-chain node does not have. Bitcoin Core's test code exceeds its production code when functional tests are included; GnB's test lines are about equal to its production lines, but concentrated in unit tests.
Every suite in the repository was executed. All pass; the defects in Section 6 exist because the suites do not exercise the relevant paths, not because tests fail.

content.v: Mutation testing of the PoW and difficulty crate

v: cargo-mutants generated 222 mutants of `crates/gnb-smh/src/{lib,difficulty}.rs`. The crate's own tests killed 176 of 213 viable mutants (82.6%). Among the 37 survivors were consensus-relevant changes: the strict PoW comparison (`<` to `<=`), `verify` and `hash` returning constants, `work` and a schedule off-by-one. Re-running the survivors against the audit harness killed 15 more, including all of those; the remaining 22 are equivalent mutants (bit-disjoint `|` vs `^`, zero-iteration loop bounds, clamp-on-equality) or mutate non-consensus accessors and `Display` implementations. With the harness, every non-equivalent consensus mutant in the crate is detected.

`audit/consistency` is a stand-alone crate (its own workspace, so the project's manifests and lockfile are untouched) that treats Bitcoin Core, BCHN and rust-bitcoin as reference implementations of the arithmetic GnB inherits from them. It uses `proptest` for property-based cases, `bitcoin` 0.32 (rust-bitcoin) as a crate oracle, `primitive-types` for 256/512-bit oracles, and the normative Python definition of GnB-SMH. All 35 tests pass.

rows: GnB accepts exactly the values Core's `DeriveTarget` accepts, decodes them to the same integers and re-encodes like `GetCompact`

Exhaustive sweep of every compact value with exponent 0..=34 (587,202,560 values) plus a sample of every larger exponent; 200,000-case proptests against Core `GetCompact` and rust-bitcoin `Target::to_compact_lossy` / `from_compact`
Zero differences. 268,435,424 encodings are accepted by both; 17,694,689 of them are non-canonical, which is safe only because consensus compares `bits` to `expected_bits` as a u32
Port of the BCHN `CalculateASERT` fixed-point step (512-bit, no truncation) with GnB's anchor convention; 100,000-case proptests on real and random anchors; 152,358-point deterministic sweep

Compact bits identical, full 256-bit targets identical; monotone in time; bounded to [1, pow_limit]; exact doubling per half-life; no panic on any (height, timestamp). Found AUD-1 (saturation for anchors near 2^256)
rust-bitcoin `merkle_tree::calculate_root` and a port of Core `ComputeMerkleRoot`
Roots identical; CVE-2012-2459 collision reproduced (GnB relies on its duplicate-transaction rule); block id unchanged when only signature bytes change
Overflow detected; total mining issuance 899,999,851,392,253 sat of 900,000,000,000,000 allocated (1.486 GNB never issued by rounding); fee function total over usize
96 random cases (header lengths 0-399, any u64 nonce, log2_n 1-12) and one canonical (2^19) case identical; reused and per-thread scratchpads leak no state
GnB's strict `out < target` pinned (Core accepts `hash == target`); `work()` never overstates and is within 2^-64 of Core for every reachable target, but differs from the Python specification (POW-6)

v: The harness is also the reason two findings exist: it measured the `work()` deviation from the specification (POW-6) and found the ASERT saturation for anchors near the pow limit (AUD-1). It should be adopted in CI; it runs in about 30 seconds in release mode.

Findings are ordered by severity. Each lists its location, the evidence status, a concrete failure scenario where applicable, the corresponding Bitcoin Core control, and a recommendation. Identifiers name the review area: POW (proof of work), DAG (GhostDAG and reorg), VAL (validation and storage), CRY (cryptography), NET (P2P, sync, RPC), WAL (wallet and web), MEM (mempool), COH (shielded pool), LED (ledger v1), ATT (attestation), OPS (CI and operations), AUD (found by the audit harness).

Each table compares a GnB component with its Bitcoin Core counterpart on design, verified-correct behaviour, weaknesses found, tests and the reviewers' scores (consensus correctness / defensive coding / test depth, 0-10).

v: Scores are 0-10 per category (10 = no material weakness found, strong preventive controls and deep tests). The weighted totals summarise code-level security only.

**Comparative note.** GnB-SMH and Bitcoin Core differ by about six points on this scale. The gap is not in cryptographic primitives or arithmetic, where GnB is competitive and in places ahead (memory-safe language, absolute-schedule difficulty that rules out timewarp, post-quantum signatures), but in the parts that took Bitcoin Core a decade of incidents to harden: connect-time validation in the correct chain context, anti-DoS ordering before expensive work, peer accounting, mempool maintenance, crash consistency, and an assurance pipeline (fuzzing, sanitizers, functional tests) that exercises all of it continuously. Closing the five Critical findings and building that pipeline are prerequisites for any further comparison.
